title: A friend at midnight (Luke 11:5–13)
hookLine: a friend knocks for bread at midnight and keeps knocking

cards: Straight after the prayer, Jesus tells a story with a very practical problem. It's midnight. A friend has turned up from a journey, tired and hungry, and there's nothing in the house to set before him.
Not a loaf. There's one option left: walk down the dark lane to a neighbor's house, where the door is shut and the children are already in bed, and knock loudly enough to be heard.

teach.b: The man at the door calls out, in the King James Bible: "Friend, lend me three loaves; For a friend of mine in his journey is come to me, and I have nothing to set before him?"

teach.h: TROUBLE ME NOT: THE DOOR IS SHUT.
teach.b: From inside comes an answer any parent of small children might give: "Trouble me not: the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give thee." But the knocking doesn't stop.
Jesus says the neighbor will get up, not because they're friends, but "because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth." Importunity is the old English word.
The Greek is anaideia: shamelessness, a nerve that doesn't care how it looks. Readers differ about whose shamelessness it is. Some hear the knocker's, refusing to give up.
Others hear the sleeper's, getting up to avoid the shame of failing a neighbor. Either way, the story isn't saying God is a grumpy neighbor who has to be nagged.

teach.h: NOT A GRUMPY GOD: HOW MUCH MORE.
teach.b: It works by contrast: if even a sleepy friend gets up at midnight, how much more will God.

teach.h: KNOCK, AND IT SHALL BE OPENED.
teach.b: Then: "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you." And Luke ends with a twist of his own. Matthew says the Father gives good things.
Luke says: "how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?" His last word here isn't bread at all, but the Holy Spirit.

how: Some Christians bring the same request to God again and again, in personal prayer, in prayer lists kept by churches, and in intercessions during Sunday worship, reading this story as permission to keep asking.

o: anger at being woken in the middle of the night
shamelessness, a nerve that won't give up
a polite and humble way of asking for help

games.q: what's inside Luke 11:5–13 — tap the pairs.

s: the story says God is like a grumpy neighbor who must be nagged
it works by contrast: if even a sleepy friend gets up, how much more will God.
the Greek word behind importunity means shamelessness
anaideia: a nerve that doesn't care how it looks.
Luke and Matthew both say the Father gives the Holy Spirit
Matthew says good things. Luke says the Holy Spirit.

games.q: you're in bed. the door is barred, the children are asleep, and your neighbor won't stop knocking for bread. what do you do?
o: grumble, then get up and give him what he needs.
shout at him to try someone else.
games.why: first comes "trouble me not," but because of the knocker's importunity, he rises and gives him as many as he needs.

practice: Think of one thing you really need that you've stopped asking for because it felt embarrassing, or greedy, or too late, and let it come to mind plainly.

If you pray, ask for it in your own words, the way you'd ask a friend, without polishing the request, and then ask again. If you don't pray, simply admit the need to yourself without apologizing for it.

wordCard.voice: Anaideia, Greek for shamelessness, nerve, which the King James Bible calls importunity: a man knocks on a barred door at midnight for three loaves and keeps knocking, and the story says, how much more will God give.

orig.note: Greek: shamelessness, nerve. the King James Bible says importunity.

carryVoice: Your line: shamelessly ask. A shut door isn't the end of this story. That's five hundred forty-four.
